resources.string: Take it as soon as you remember
Still inside the window — inject as soon as you can
Past the window — contact your doctor first
It is only about %1$d minutes past the scheduled time, so take it as soon as you remember.
It is only about %1$s hours past the scheduled time, so take it as soon as you remember.
If your next dose is nearly due, skip this one — **never take two doses at once**.
Log the catch-up dose in today\'s check-in as usual, so your adherence record stays accurate.
It is about %1$d minutes past the scheduled time; best to skip this dose and take the next one as planned.
It is about %1$s hours past the scheduled time; best to skip this dose and take the next one as planned.
**Never double the dose** to make up for it — doubling raises the risk of side effects.
If you miss doses often (several times a week, for example), talk to your doctor about adjusting the plan or switching to a form with more frequent reminders.
About %1$d minutes past the scheduled time — still inside the usual catch-up window (%2$d hours).
About %1$s hours past the scheduled time — still inside the usual catch-up window (%2$d hours).
Inject as soon as possible, then shift the next injection to keep the **original interval** — do not bring it forward.
Immunosuppressants / biologics: if the injection is several days late, or you are unsure whether to catch up, phone your rheumatology team first.
If you feel unwell after the catch-up injection, contact your doctor promptly.
It is more than %1$d hours past the scheduled time (about %2$d minutes), beyond the usual catch-up window.
It is more than %1$d hours past the scheduled time (about %2$s hours), beyond the usual catch-up window.
**Contact your rheumatology team first** to confirm the catch-up plan (whether to catch up, when to do it, and whether the interval changes).
Do not double the dose or shorten the interval yourself before your doctor confirms.
Interrupting biologics / immunosuppressants may affect disease control, so the sooner you talk to your doctor the better.
Any adjustment must follow your treating physician\'s instructions.
Medication (includes immunosuppressants — infection risk): %1$s, %2$d in total

Smoking is a risk factor for spinal inflammation and disease progression in axSpA, so stopping is advised (your doctor can help you plan how). An honest note: guidelines recommend stopping because of the known health risks of smoking; dedicated evidence that it improves axSpA outcomes is still lacking.
Having stopped smoking is a clear plus — keep it up; it also lowers cardiovascular risk (which is already higher in people with AS).
You sit for about %1$d hours a day: get up and move for 2–3 minutes every 30–45 minutes, which counters stiffness better than one long session.
You sleep about %1$d hours on average, which is on the short side: too little sleep amplifies pain and morning stiffness, so keep today\'s intensity moderate and put regularity first.
No exercise habit at present: start with the L1 gentle items and build up to 3–5 times a week first, then talk about duration and intensity.
You already exercise regularly: progress steadily — duration first (add 5–10 minutes every 1–2 weeks), then frequency, then intensity.
Do one round of gentle items after getting up, and start the day\'s plan once the stiffness eases.

Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes often points to active inflammation. Do one round of gentle items after getting up before starting the day\'s plan, and watch that trend; if it lasts several days in a row, tell your doctor at the next appointment.
Previous lab reports / imaging reports (paper copies, or the attachments archived in this app)
Current medication list (this app can export an emergency card / follow-up report PDF)
If blood is being taken that day: come fasting (no food for 8–12 hours beforehand; a little water is fine — follow the hospital\'s requirements)
If imaging is planned that day: remove metal jewellery and bring previous scans for comparison
For reference only; follow your treating physician\'s instructions.
This app is a personal health record tool. It does not constitute medical advice and cannot replace diagnosis or treatment by a doctor.
Always follow your treating physician\'s instructions on medication and treatment; any adjustment is subject to those instructions.
All health data stays on this device and is never uploaded to any server.
This app is not a medical device; its records and prompts are not used for diagnosis or treatment decisions.
Keep the spine in a neutral position and avoid holding the same flexed posture for long periods (slumped sitting, looking down at a phone).
Sit on a firm chair with a backrest; if needed, put a small cushion behind the lower back to keep the lumbar curve. When standing, keep your weight even and look straight ahead.
Lie on your back or on your side; keep the pillow low (side-lying: about the width of one shoulder; back-lying: a thin pillow).
A firm, supportive mattress is best; avoid one that is too soft.
Lying face down is not advised — it twists the neck and does not help the spine extend; people with AS should especially avoid it.
